## Recall: Grammar of ggplot2

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/lessons/img_slides/ggplot_layers.png){fig-align="center" width="1600"}
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
- We typically start at the bottom (data) and work our way up (themes)
  - You skip some of the layers if you don't need them

 

-   `ggplot2` needs at least the following three to produce a chart:
    -   data, a mapping, and a layer

 

-   For the most part, there are default settings for the other parts:
    -   scales, facets, coordinates, and themes
:::
:::::

## Recall: common components of `ggplot2`

::: columns
::: column
- Common components of `ggplot2` include: 
  - `ggplot()`: the main function to create a plot
  - `aes()`: the function to specify the mapping of variables to axes
  - `geom_*()` or `stat_*()`: functions to add layers to the plot
  - `labs()`: the function to change labels of axes and title
  - `theme()`: the function to adjust non-data plot elements such as text size,
:::
::: column

 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  data = my_data, 
  mapping = aes(x = col1, y = col2)
  ) +  #<1>       
  
  geom_*() +          
  
  labs() +       
  
  theme()                                  
```
:::

:::
:::

::: blue
::: blue-cont
In this lesson, we will focus on **using different geometric objects** and **building the mapping**.
:::
:::

## Geometric objects

- Geometric objects (`geom`'s) are used to represent the datapoints (aka observations)
  - The same variable's data can be represented in different ways

[**For example:** we can plot Age vs. Income using a scatterplot or a smoothed line]{style="color: #EF85B3;"}

::: columns
::: column

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Scatterplot of Age vs. Income"}
ggplot(
  hrs_data, 
  mapping = aes(
    x = age_yr, 
    y = income
    )
  ) + 
  geom_point() +
  ylim(0, 2000000)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960}
:::
:::

:::
::: column

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Line plot of Age vs. Income"}
ggplot(
  hrs_data, 
  mapping = aes(
    x = age_yr, 
    y = income
    )
  ) + 
  geom_smooth() +
  ylim(0, 2000000)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960}
:::
:::

:::
:::

## Types of geoms

- Check out `ggplot2` cheatsheet for a [list of common `geom_*()` functions](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/data-visualization.html#geoms)

::: columns
::: column

::: blue
::: blue-ttl
Common `geom_*()` for plots with **one variable**:
:::
::: blue-cont
- `geom_histogram()` (for numeric)
- `geom_bar()` (for categorical)
- `geom_boxplot()`
- `geom_density()`
- `geom_dotplot()`
:::
:::
:::
::: column

::: green
::: green-ttl
Common `geom_*()` for plots with **two or more variables**:
:::
::: green-cont
- `geom_point()`
- `geom_line()`
- `geom_boxplot()`
- `geom_smooth()`
- `geom_jitter()`

:::
:::
:::
:::

## Example 1: One continuous variable (1/2)

::: columns
::: column

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(hrs_00) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = age_yr)) #<1>
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


1. The `geom_histogram()` function is used to create a histogram of the `age_yr` variable.
:::
::: column

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(hrs_00) +
  geom_density(aes(x = age_yr)) #<2>
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


2. The `geom_density()` function is used to create a density plot of the `age_yr` variable.
:::
:::

## Example 1: One continuous variable (2/2)

::: columns
::: column

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(hrs_00) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = age_yr)) #<3>
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


3. The `geom_boxplot()` function is used to create a boxplot of the `age_yr` variable.
:::
::: column

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(hrs_00) +
  geom_dotplot(aes(x = age_yr)) #<4>
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


4. The `geom_dotplot()` function is used to create a dot plot of the `age_yr` variable.
:::
:::

## Example 2: One continuous, one categorical variable (1/2)

::: columns
::: column

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(hrs_00) +
  geom_boxplot( #<1>
    aes(x = age_yr, y = srh)
    ) #<1>
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


1. The `geom_boxplot()` function is used to create a boxplot of the `age_yr` variable (on the x-axis), grouped by the `srh` variable (on the y-axis).
:::
::: column

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(hrs_00) +
  geom_jitter( #<2>
    aes(x = age_yr, y = srh)
    ) #<2>
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


2. The `geom_jitter()` function is used to create a scatterplot of the `age_yr` variable (on the x-axis), grouped by the `srh` variable (on the y-axis). The points are jittered (spaced apart) to avoid overplotting.
:::
:::

## Example 2: One continuous, one categorical variable (1/2)

::: columns
::: column

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(ggridges) #<1>
ggplot(hrs_00) +
  geom_density_ridges( #<2>
    aes(x = age_yr, y = srh)
    ) #<2>
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


1. The `ggridges` package is needed for the `geom_density_ridges()` function.
2. We can use `geom_density_ridges()` to create a density plots of the `age_yr` variable (on the x-axis), grouped by the `srh` variable (on the y-axis). The density plots are stacked on top of each other to create a ridge plot. 
:::
::: column

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  hrs_00, 
  aes(x = age_yr, y = srh) #<3>
  ) +
  geom_boxplot() + #<4>
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2) #<5>
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


3. We can move `aes()` into `ggplot()` since both `geom_boxplot()` and `geom_jitter()` use the same mapping
4. We can add a boxplot
5. Then we can stack a jitter plot on top of the boxplot to show the individual data points. The `alpha` argument is used to make the points more transparent.
:::
:::

## Aesthetic mapping/setting

- If we want to change the visual properties of the plotted data, we use **aesthetic mapping/setting**
  - This is not about the design choices of the figure, but the aesthetics of the **data representation**

- Here are a list of common aesthetic options (from the [Epi Handbook](https://epirhandbook.com/en/new_pages/ggplot_basics.html#plot-aesthetics)):
  - `x` = The x-axis variable
  - `y` = The y-axis variable
  - `shape` = Display a point with geom_point() as a dot, star, triangle, or square…
  - `fill` = The interior color (e.g. of a bar or boxplot)
  - `color` = The exterior line of a bar, boxplot, etc., or the point color if using geom_point()
  - `size` = Size (e.g. line thickness, point size)
  - `alpha` = Transparency (1 = opaque, 0 = invisible)
  - `binwidth` = Width of histogram bins (for `geom_histogram()` only)
  - `width` = Width of bar plot columns (for `geom_bar()` only)
  - `linetype` = Line type (e.g. solid, dashed, dotted)
  
## Example 3: Scatterplot of age vs. self-reported health

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Original scatterplot of age vs. self-reported health"}
ggplot(
  hrs_00,
  aes(x = age_yr, y = srh)
  ) +
  geom_jitter()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Scatterplot with changed data aesthetics"}
ggplot(
  hrs_00, 
  aes(x = age_yr, y = srh)
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
      color = "darkgreen", #<1>
      size = 0.5, #<2>
      alpha = 0.2 #<3>
    )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


1. We changed the color of the points to dark green
2. We changed the size of the points to 0.5 (smaller than the default size of 1)
3. We changed the transparency of the points to 0.2 (more transparent than the default alpha of 1)

:::
:::

## Example 4: Barplot of self-rated health


::: {.cell output-location='column'}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  hrs_00, 
  aes(x = srh)
  ) +
  geom_bar(
    color = "black", #<1>
    fill = "lightblue", #<2>
    width = 0.5 #<3>
    )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


1. We changed the color of the bars to black (color is the outline of the bars)
2. We changed the fill color of the bars to light blue
3. We changed the width of the bars to 0.5 (we would use `binwidth` for `geom_histogram()`)

## BIG WARNING!

**Color is often NOT needed in a plot!!**

- In general, when you add color, you should **adding** information to the plot, not just for aesthetics
- And that color should not be conveyed by existing text

![](../img_slides/jurassic_park.png){fig-align="center" width="400"}
  
## Two ways of setting aesthetics

::: columns
::: {.column width="47%"}
::: pink2
::: pink2-ttl
Outside `aes()` (aesthetic setting)
:::
::: pink2-cont
- This is what we've been doing so far
- We set the aesthetics of the data to a specific value 
  - Like `darkgreen` or `0.5`
- These settings are **not** based on the data

For example: 

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  hrs_00,
  aes(x = age_yr, y = srh)
  ) +
  geom_jitter(color = "darkgreen") #<1>
```
:::


1. `darkgreen` is a specific value within `geom_jitter()` but not in `aes()`
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="53%"}
::: red
::: red-ttl
Inside `aes()` (aesthetic mapping)
:::
::: red-cont
- We can also set the aesthetics of the data based on the data itself
- Let's say we want the type of dots to be based on the self-reported health variable
  - We can do this by putting the `shape` aesthetic inside `aes()`

For example:

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  hrs_00,
  aes(x = age_yr, y = srh, color = srh) #<2>
  ) +
  geom_jitter()
```
:::


2. Now we put `color = srh` inside `aes()` so that the color of the dots is based on the self-reported health variable
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Example outside and inside `aes()`

::: columns
::: {.column width="47%"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  hrs_00,
  aes(x = age_yr, y = srh)
  ) +
  geom_jitter(color = "darkgreen")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


:::

::: {.column width="53%"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  hrs_00,
  aes(x = age_yr, y = srh, color = srh)
  ) +
  geom_jitter()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


:::
:::

## Better example of fill/color

- Color is good when it adds information to the plot
- This is helpful when we want to compare the distribution of different categories
  - For example: distribution of age in our dataset between males and females


::: {.cell output-location='column'}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  hrs_00,
  aes(
    x = age_yr, 
    fill = sex
    )
  ) +
  geom_histogram()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Data_viz_Basic_plotting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


## Wrap-up

- We can use different geometric objects to represent data in different ways
- Some geometric objects only work for certain types of data than others

 

- We can set aesthetics of datapoints in `ggplot2`
  - Including color, fill, size, transparency, shape, and more

 

- Color should add information to our plots!

## Resources

- [`ggplot2` Cheatsheet in html form](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/data-visualization.html)
- [`ggplot2` Cheatsheet in pdf form](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/data-visualization.pdf)
- [Wall Street Journal Guide to Information Graphics](https://books.google.com/books/about/The_Wall_Street_Journal_Guide_to_Informa.html?id=NlqNEAAAQBAJ&source=kp_book_description)

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
